title: Efficacy Starts With the Institution, Not the Tool
author: Phil Hill
summary: Phil Hill returns to the University of Maryland study of an AI course assistant, which he and Morgan Hill had already criticized for barely testing tutoring. A recent interview with Provost Jennifer King Rice reveals a deeper problem: she was the report's senior author and the person who set up the initiative, so the leadership decisions behind it belong inside the analysis. UMD supplied extensive technical documentation but no guidance on how instructors should fold the tool into teaching, and only about 15 percent of students offered the tool used it. Hill argues the finding that unguided access did not work was a foreseeable design flaw rather than a research discovery, since the report itself says effects depend on scaffolding and realized engagement. He replaces the simple model of tool, outcome, evidence with a longer chain that includes problem definition, faculty support, student use, and adaptation. The conclusion is that implementation and efficacy cannot be separated, and academic leaders who demand evidence from vendors should hold their own decisions to the same standard.
points: Hill's central move is to shift scrutiny from the technology to the institution that deployed it, noting that the provost who ran the study also set up the initiative being evaluated.
The Maryland rollout offered heavy technical documentation but no instructional guidance, so no responding instructor reported using the tool in assignments, which makes null results unsurprising.
The report's own statement that effects depend on configuration, scaffolding, and engagement shows the authors knew what conditions were required and still designed an initiative without them.

He proposes a realistic efficacy chain running from problem definition through tool selection, faculty support, student awareness, and measurement before outcomes, instead of the simple tool-to-outcome model.

The practical test for leaders is whether they defined an educational purpose, supported instructors, and responded to weak adoption, because randomization does not excuse skipped implementation work.
quotes: UMD billed its study as a test of AI tutoring, but it largely tested access to an answer-giving chatbot with little integration into teaching.
But the core implementation choice is that UMD provided “no additional guidance for how [instructors] should incorporate the tool.
This is EdTech 101. Tools are only valuable in supporting student learning if they are integrated into instructional practices.
This was not a research discovery; it was a foreseeable flaw in the design of the initiative.
But it does mean that implementation and efficacy cannot be separated.
Leaving faculty and students to figure things out for themselves is an implementation strategy—a spectacularly bad one.
Academic leaders who demand evidence that EdTech works should expect the same scrutiny of their own decisions.
